Statistics Canada Web Data Service complete table inventory via getAllCubesListLite (https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/wds/rest/getAllCubesListLite, cited by Claude): systematically verified across all 8,269 released data tables that Statistics Canada publishes no table containing a cycling participation rate for the City of Edmonton or Edmonton CMA, bounding the absence of representative participation data.

Statistics Canada Daily table "Main mode of commuting for the 10 largest census metropolitan areas, May 2021 to May 2025" (https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/daily-quotidien/250826/t002a-eng.htm, cited by GPT): evaluated the StatCan table specifically referenced by commenters and verified that it measures journey-to-work commuting modes rather than an all-trips mode share.
errors_in_other_reviews: GPT's review of claim "cycling-trips-1-3-million-2026" citing developer API documentation "https://dev.socrata.com/foundry/data.edmonton.ca/tq23-qn4m": Citation does not say what the reviewer claims (and wrong source). GPT consulted developer foundry documentation metadata showing "last updated 2026-07-22" and concluded the base dataset did not cover the full required period through 2026-07-31, erroneously returning a procedural verdict of Not established under the short-window rule. The live City of Edmonton Socrata open dataset at https://data.edmonton.ca/resource/tq23-qn4m.json has rowsUpdatedAt of 2026-09-03 22:53 UTC and contains continuous records through 2026-09-02; the required 2026-01-01 through 2026-07-31 window is complete, recording 1,291,714 bicycle counts (Supported).

GPT's review of claim "bike-lanes-look-empty" citing "https://edmonton.ca/sites/default/files/public-files/BikePlan-ImplementationGuide.pdf" (The Bike Plan Implementation Guide 2021–2026): Methodological deviation and wrong instrument. GPT failed to execute the brief's mandatory 5-test spatial join protocol against open datasets tq23-qn4m and vd4b-a4iv for July 2025 daily medians. Instead, GPT substituted historical annual counts from 2021 (205,000 at 83 Ave / 99 St = ~562/day) and multi-location June 2017/2018 counts from an old PDF implementation guide, sidestepping the empirical evaluation of the 20 metered on-street counters in service in July 2025.

GPT's review of claim "one-percent-year-round-users" citing "https://why.edmonton.ca/stories/cycling-in-a-winter-wonderland" (City of Edmonton webpage "Cycling in a winter wonderland"): Wrong denominator error. GPT cited a City webpage claiming "an estimated one in four cyclists rides all year" as challenging evidence against the 1% year-round ceiling. This figure divides by active cyclists (25% of cyclists) rather than all Edmonton residents, committing a wrong-denominator error; 25% of a small cycling minority is fully consistent with under 1% of the total population.

Claude's review of claim "riders-are-recreational-not-commuters" citing "https://edmonton.ca/public-files/assets/document?path=PDF%2F2015_HTS_SummaryReport.pdf" (2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey Summary Report, Table 3-10): Priority rule violation and unsupported derivation. Claude derived bicycle commute vs recreational trips (~21,379 work vs ~11,994 recreation) by multiplying rounded integer modal shares (3% HB-Work, 1% NHB-Work, 3% HB-Social/Rec) by all-mode category totals, and used this to contradict the claim. The brief's threshold ladder explicitly mandates: "Apply in this order: Not established if no published Edmonton source breaks bicycle trips down by purpose, or if the source's categories cannot be mapped completely onto recreation and commuting. Say what the obstacle is." Table 3-10 does not publish bicycle trips broken down by purpose, and the survey's categories include School, Post-Secondary Education, Shopping, and Personal Business that cannot be mapped to recreation or commuting. Reaching a substantive Contradicted verdict via reviewer arithmetic on rounded modal shares bypasses the mandatory priority rule requiring Not established.

GPT's review of claim "riders-are-recreational-not-commuters" citing "https://edmonton.ca/sites/default/files/public-files/2015_HTS_SummaryReport.pdf" (2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey Summary Report, Table 3-10): Priority rule violation and unsupported derivation. Like Claude, GPT derived ~21,379 work-related trips and ~11,994 recreational trips from rounded integer modal shares and all-mode category counts to argue commuting outweighs recreation. Because Table 3-10 does not report bicycle trips by purpose and the survey categories cannot be mapped completely onto recreation and commuting, the brief's first-order priority rule requiring Not established was erroneously bypassed.

claims.proposition_evaluated: Edmonton's automated counters recorded nearly 1.3 million cycling trips in the first seven months of 2026.
claims.interpretation_notes: Evaluated as the aggregate sum of total_cyclist_count recorded across every City of Edmonton automated bicycle counter published in open dataset tq23-qn4m between 2026-01-01T00:00:00 and 2026-07-31T23:59:59 inclusive. Counters record sensor detections (labeled 'counts' by the City), not individual unique trips or persons. The live dataset covers the required window in full (rows updated 2026-09-03, data through 2026-09-02), recording exactly 1,291,714 bicycle counts across 48 reporting counter locations (41 recorded non-zero cyclist counts; 7 are pedestrian-only). Under both the primary threshold ([1.10M, 1.50M]) and the alternative tenth-range threshold ([1.17M, 1.43M]), the recorded figure of 1,291,714 counts falls squarely within the Supported band (within 0.64% of 1.3 million). In cross-review, we note that GPT returned Not established by citing developer foundry doc metadata (dev.socrata.com/foundry/...) showing an update date of 2026-07-22; this was an error because the live dataset itself is complete through 2026-07-31. Media tracking confirms the circulating sentence originated from a CBC News analysis (2026-08-07) of the same open dataset.

supporting_evidence.finding: The City of Edmonton's automated bicycle counters recorded an aggregate total of 1,291,714 cyclist counts between 2026-01-01T00:00:00.000 and 2026-07-31T23:59:59.999 across 48 reporting counters, directly confirming 'nearly 1.3 million'.
supporting_evidence.establishes: Establishes the exact measured bicycle count (1,291,714) recorded by automated sensors across Edmonton's active network over the seven-month period.

supporting_evidence.finding: Counter metadata shows 48 distinct sensor locations reported during the 2026 window, led by High Level Bridge West which recorded 127,740 counts (9.89% of the network total).
supporting_evidence.establishes: Establishes counter location descriptions, spatial coordinates, and monitoring configurations.

supporting_evidence.finding: CBC News, analysing the same City open data from 2019-01-01 to 2026-07-31, reported 'nearly 1.3 million trips have happened through the first seven months of 2026', establishing the media origin of the commenter's exact phrasing. CBC noted the City identified an unintentional sensor swap between pedestrians and cyclists at three sites (most notably Queen Elizabeth Park) affecting 2021 and 2022 only.

challenging_evidence.finding: The City of Edmonton explicitly notes that automated counter data is raw, unverified, and subject to sensor outages; in the Jan-Jul 2026 window, 7 counters missed days, totaling 383 missing counter-days out of 10,176 potential days (96.2% completeness).

limitations: Counters record sensor detections (passages), not individual trips or unique persons; one person commuting both ways past one counter generates two counts, and passing multiple counters on a single journey increments each.

Data is uncalibrated raw output from Eco-Counter hardware without routine validation against manual control counts.

The rate of sensor occlusions, hardware drift, or missed counts during heavy snow or bunching.

claims.proposition_evaluated: The Edmonton bike lanes that are metered, including the lanes residents named as empty, carry little or no bicycle traffic.
claims.interpretation_notes: Evaluated using the brief's revised five-test rule for metered on-street bike lanes. Test 1 found 51 cyclist counter locations in tq23-qn4m (10 pedestrian-only removed). Test 2 confirmed 42 in service on 2025-07-01 (9 removed). Test 3 spatial join to built Bike Routes vd4b-a4iv identified 21 ON ROAD and 21 OFF ROAD counters (0 unclassifiable, 0 borderline under the 10m rule; smallest gap was 20.8m at High Level Bridge East). Test 4 (revised) removed 1 out-of-service counter (106 Street N of Jasper Avenue, last record 2025-07-16, last complete month June 2025 median 177.5). Test 5 confirmed all 20 remaining counters reported all 31 days of July 2025 (0 under-reported). July 2025 daily medians ranged from 46.0 to 979.0 bikes/day. Under the primary cutoff of 25 bikes/day, zero counters were below 25, resulting in Contradicted. Under the alternative cutoff of 50 bikes/day, exactly one counter (96 Street S of Jasper Ave at 46.0) fell below 50 while 19 exceeded 50, which would yield Partially supported.

supporting_evidence.finding: One metered on-street counter (96 Street S of Jasper Ave) recorded a July 2025 median of 46.0 bicycles per day (busiest day 68), which falls below the alternative threshold of 50 bicycles per day.
supporting_evidence.establishes: Establishes that the lowest-volume metered on-street lane carries roughly 3 bicycles per hour over a 16-hour day.

supporting_evidence.finding: The only City count published on Whyte Avenue itself is short-duration and historical: dataset e8q6-8tts ('Bike Counts - Historic') recorded 141-187 two-way bicycles over 24 hours on 82 Avenue east/west of 104 Street on 2016-09-27/28.

supporting_evidence.establishes: Establishes that Whyte Avenue itself has no automated counter, and its only manual counts are from 2016.

challenging_evidence.finding: Zero of the 20 measured on-street bike lane counters had a July 2025 daily median below the primary threshold of 25 bicycles per day. challenging_evidence.establishes: Directly contradicts the claim that metered on-street lanes carry little or no bicycle traffic during peak summer riding season.

limitations: The finding applies strictly to the 20 metered on-street bike lanes; Edmonton's unmetered bike lanes were not measured.

claims.proposition_evaluated: No more than about 2 percent of Edmonton's population rides a bicycle.
claims.interpretation_notes: Evaluated as the proportion of Edmonton residents who rode a bicycle at least once during a 12-month reference period, measured by a representative probability sample of Edmonton residents. No such representative survey exists in the published record. Statistics Canada's Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS) collects 12-month cycling participation data, but releases public data only at the health region level (Edmonton Zone), not for the City of Edmonton CSD or CMA. A comprehensive search of Statistics Canada's 8,269 released data tables confirmed zero municipal cycling participation tables. Travel surveys (2015 HTS) measure 24-hour trips, not individual annual participation. The City's 2014 bike ridership survey used the opt-in Edmonton Insight Community panel (62% rode at least once/year), which is non-representative. Under the brief's explicit instructions, the absence of any representative population survey measuring cycling participation mandates a verdict of Not established. Two circulating claims regarding bike-lane users ('.001%' and '500 people') represent unmeasured lane-specific metrics that cannot be evaluated with general population participation data. Claude, Gemini, and GPT all independently reached Not established on this claim.

supporting_evidence.finding: In public discussions and municipal planning documents, cycling modal share is commonly cited in the 1% to 2% range, but this figure is derived from Journey to Work census commuting data (0.88%) or travel survey mode share (1.7%), not population participation.
supporting_evidence.source_title: Bicycle ridership and intention in a northern, low-cycling city
supporting_evidence.establishes: Establishes that academic literature on Edmonton utility cycling references low overall modal shares but relies on non-probability panel data.

challenging_evidence.finding: The City of Edmonton's August 2014 bike ridership survey (N=816) found that 59.9% of respondents reported riding a bicycle at least once a year, but the survey was administered via the opt-in Edmonton Insight Community and an open link, making it non-representative.
challenging_evidence.source_title: Bike Ridership - Edmonton Insight Community, dataset nhbh-yj57
challenging_evidence.establishes: Demonstrates that existing municipal survey instruments measuring riding frequency rely on opt-in panels rather than representative sampling.

challenging_evidence.finding: A comprehensive search of Statistics Canada's Web Data Service catalog (all 8,269 cubes) and CCHS public-use documentation identified zero published representative tables measuring annual cycling participation at the City of Edmonton or Edmonton CMA level.
challenging_evidence.source_title: Statistics Canada Web Data Service, getAllCubesListLite; CCHS Questionnaire
challenging_evidence.establishes: Confirms that representative 12-month cycling participation rates for Edmonton residents are not published.

limitations: Participation rate (people who ride) and bike-lane usage (people who use lanes) are distinct measures; no instrument measures distinct lane users.
Shared methodology: Claim 3 and Claim 4 evaluate population participation from the same absent representative survey family.
The finding reflects a true absence in the published record: no probability-sample survey measuring 12-month cycling participation in Edmonton has been released.
unknowns: The true percentage of Edmonton residents who ride a bicycle at least once per year.
The number of unique residents who utilize municipal bike lanes.

missing_evidence.description: A representative probability-sample survey of Edmonton residents measuring 12-month cycling participation.
missing_evidence.likely_holder: Statistics Canada (via custom CCHS microdata tabulation) or City of Edmonton

claims.proposition_evaluated: No more than 1 percent of Edmonton's population rides a bicycle year-round, and fewer than 15 percent ride in the rest of the year.
claims.interpretation_notes: Evaluated against representative population surveys reporting seasonal cycling participation for Edmonton residents (Part A: year-round <= 2.0%; Part B: non-winter < 15%). As established in Claim 3, no representative survey measures seasonal cycling participation for Edmonton. The 2014 Insight Community bike survey (nhbh-yj57) and academic analysis (Urban Geography, 2016) reported 10.2% year-round and 47.4% warm-weather cycling, but this sample is an opt-in panel and inadmissible for population estimates. Automated counters show a sharp winter decline (winter accounts for only 4.87% of annual counts), but counter passages cannot substitute for individual participation rates. City marketing claims that 'one in four cyclists rides all year' commit a wrong denominator error (dividing by cyclists rather than all residents). Because no representative survey measures Edmonton seasonal cycling participation, the brief's priority rule mandates Not established. Claude, Gemini, and GPT all independently returned Not established.

supporting_evidence.finding: Automated counters demonstrate a dramatic seasonal drop in cycling traffic during winter: in calendar year 2025, winter months (December, January, February) accounted for only 139,245 of 2,856,631 annual counts (4.87%), and January alone accounted for 60,847 counts (2.13%), consistent with a very small year-round riding core.
supporting_evidence.establishes: Establishes the seasonal volume drop in counter passages, though counter passages cannot substitute for individual participation rates.

challenging_evidence.finding: The 2014 Edmonton Insight Community bike ridership survey (nhbh-yj57) reported that 10.2% of panel respondents (66 of 646) cycled year-round and 47.4% (306 of 646) cycled in warm weather only, but these figures derive from an opt-in panel and cannot establish population prevalence.
challenging_evidence.source_title: Bike Ridership - Edmonton Insight Community; Urban Geography
challenging_evidence.source_publisher: City of Edmonton Open Data Portal
challenging_evidence.establishes: Shows that opt-in panel data yields rates far exceeding both ceilings, but is methodologically inadmissible.

challenging_evidence.finding: A City of Edmonton webpage states that an estimated 'one in four cyclists rides all year', which represents roughly 25% of active cyclists rather than all Edmonton residents.
challenging_evidence.establishes: Illustrates circulating municipal claims but commits a wrong denominator error by dividing by cyclists rather than total population.

limitations: Neither seasonal participation rate (year-round or warm-weather) is measured by any representative Edmonton survey.
Shared methodology: Claim 3 and Claim 4 evaluate population participation from the same absent representative survey family.
Counter volume seasonal drops (4.87% in winter) describe sensor passage distributions, not unique resident participation rates.
unknowns: The true proportion of Edmonton residents who ride in winter versus warm weather.
The proportion of winter cyclists who use protected lanes versus arterial roadways or off-street paths.

missing_evidence.description: A representative seasonal travel or physical activity survey measuring winter and warm-weather cycling participation.
missing_evidence.likely_holder: City of Edmonton or Statistics Canada

Part B ceiling: < 15.0% of Edmonton population (unmeasured in representative data).

claims.proposition_evaluated: About 2 percent of all trips in Edmonton are made by bicycle.
claims.interpretation_notes: Evaluated against the most recent published regional travel survey on the as-of date: the 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey (HTS) Summary Report. Bicycles accounted for 1.7% of all weekday daily trips made by City of Edmonton residents (54,800 of 3,139,100 total trips). Under the brief's thresholds, 1.7% falls within the primary Supported range of [1.5%, 2.5%] and the alternative range of [1.2%, 3.0%]. Required alternative geography: across the broader Capital Region, the bicycle mode share was 0.8% (10,600 of 1,331,800 trips), which is geography-sensitive. The successor survey, Navigating Tomorrow, launched in September 2025 but had released no results as of the freeze date (2026-09-03). The commenter's cited Statistics Canada table ('Main mode of commuting for the 10 largest census metropolitan areas', 250826/t002a-eng.htm) measures journey-to-work commuting, not all trips. All panel reviewers (Claude, Gemini, GPT) concur on Supported.

supporting_evidence.finding: The 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey Summary Report establishes that bicycles accounted for 1.7% of all weekday daily trips made by City of Edmonton residents (54,800 of 3,139,100 trips), directly matching 'about 2 percent'.
supporting_evidence.source_title: 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey Overview
supporting_evidence.establishes: Establishes the municipal trip mode share for bicycles (1.7%) across 3.14 million weekday trips by Edmonton residents.

supporting_evidence.finding: Historical HTS data shows bicycle mode share grew from 0.4% (10,100 trips) in 1994 to 0.9% (25,300 trips) in 2005 and 1.7% (54,800 trips) in 2015, making cycling the fastest-growing mode.
supporting_evidence.source_title: 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey Summary Report, Table 3-2 and Figure 3-4
supporting_evidence.establishes: Establishes long-term upward trajectory in cycling mode share prior to major network expansions.

challenging_evidence.finding: Across the entire Capital Region, the 2015 Household Travel Survey recorded a bicycle mode share of 0.8% of daily trips (10,600 of 1,331,800 trips by regional residents outside Edmonton).
challenging_evidence.source_title: 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey Overview
challenging_evidence.establishes: Establishes the required regional alternative bicycle mode share (0.8%), demonstrating geographic sensitivity.

challenging_evidence.finding: The published 1.7% figure is eleven years old (measured in fall 2015), representing travel patterns prior to substantial bike network expansion and the COVID-19 pandemic.
challenging_evidence.establishes: Notes that 2015 data is dated and that continuous monitoring began under Navigating Tomorrow in 2025.

claims.proposition_evaluated: Fewer than 1 percent of Edmonton commuters travel to work by bicycle, according to 2021 census figures.
claims.interpretation_notes: Evaluated against the 2021 Census of Population, Journey to Work (reference week May 2-8, 2021), for employed persons aged 15 and over with a usual place of work or no fixed workplace address (excluding workers who worked at home). For the City of Edmonton (Census subdivision), 3,355 commuters gave bicycle as their main mode of commuting out of 380,315 commuters, representing 0.882% (rounds to 0.88% or 0.9%). This is strictly below 1.0%, satisfying both the primary (<1.0%) and alternative (<1.1%) Supported thresholds. Required alternative geography: for the Edmonton Census Metropolitan Area (CMA), 3,905 of 537,645 commuters traveled by bicycle (0.726%, rounds to 0.73%), which is also below 1.0%. Pre-pandemic baseline context: in the 2016 Census, 5,575 of 466,230 City commuters cycled (1.196%, rounds to 1.20%), which would have been Partially supported. Pandemic context: 102,210 City workers worked at home (21.12% of the place-of-work universe of 483,855); if home workers are included in the denominator, the bicycle share drops to 0.69% (3,355 of 483,855). Municipal comparison: the 2012 municipal census (dataset 24yu-behb) recorded 2,568 cycling commuters out of 380,640 (0.67%). In round 2, Gemini corrects its round 1 mention of 4,600 / 1.1% to the exact census count of 5,575 / 1.20%. All panel reviewers concur on Supported.

claims.proposition_evaluated: 87 percent of Edmontonians commute by car.
claims.interpretation_notes: Evaluated as the share of commuters whose main mode of commuting is car, truck, or van (as driver or passenger) in the 2021 Census for employed persons aged 15+ with a usual place of work or no fixed workplace. For the City of Edmonton (CSD), 323,705 commuters commuted by car (298,320 drivers and 25,380 passengers) out of 380,315 commuters, equaling 85.11%. This falls within the primary Supported band [84%, 90%] and the alternative band [82%, 92%]. Required alternative geography: for the Edmonton Census Metropolitan Area (CMA), 469,900 commuters traveled by car (437,695 drivers and 32,210 passengers) out of 537,645 commuters, equaling 87.40%, which rounds directly to 87%. The circulating figure of 87% matches the regional CMA figure almost exactly, but represents a fair description of the City figure (85.11%) within brief thresholds. Driver-only alternative: 78.44% in the City (298,320 of 380,315) and 81.41% in the CMA. Full mode breakdown (City CSD, denominator 380,315): Car/truck/van 323,705 (85.11%), Sustainable 47,640 (12.53%) [Transit 30,860 (8.11%), Walk 13,430 (3.53%), Bike 3,355 (0.88%)], Motorcycle 335 (0.09%), Other 8,635 (2.27%), summing to 100.00%. Pre-pandemic 2016 comparison: 367,225 of 466,230 = 78.76%. If workers at home (102,210) are included in the denominator (total 483,855), the car share is 66.90%. All panel reviewers concur on Supported.

claims.proposition_evaluated: Most cycling in Edmonton is recreational rather than commuting.
claims.interpretation_notes: Tested against the most recent published household travel survey (2015 HTS) and municipal datasets under the brief's ordered threshold ladder: 'Apply in this order: Not established if no published Edmonton source breaks bicycle trips down by purpose, or if the source's categories cannot be mapped completely onto recreation and commuting. Say what the obstacle is.' The 2015 HTS Summary Report does not publish a breakdown of bicycle trips by purpose. Table 3-10 only breaks down all trips across all modes by purpose and reports integer-rounded bicycle mode shares within each purpose (e.g. 3% for HB-Work, 1% for NHB-Work, 3% for HB-Social/Rec). Furthermore, the survey categories include HB-School, HB-Post Secondary (HB-PSE), HB-Shopping, and HB-Personal Business, which cannot be mapped completely onto recreation and commuting. Under the brief's first priority condition, the lack of a published purpose breakdown and the inability to map categories completely mandates Not established. In cross-review, we evaluate the alternative approach taken by Claude and GPT, who multiplied the rounded mode shares by total purpose trips in Table 3-10 to estimate trip counts: ~21,379 work trips (37.8%-39.0%) vs ~11,994 social/recreational trips (21.2%-21.9%). If this reviewer-derived arithmetic is accepted, commuting trips exceed recreational trips (Com > Rec), which would yield Contradicted. In no reading is the claim Supported. Counter temporal profiles show protected bike lanes exhibit pronounced weekday morning (08:00) and afternoon (16:00-17:00) peaks, with weekday volumes exceeding weekend volumes by 40-87%, confirming substantial utility commuter traffic.

supporting_evidence.finding: The City's August 2014 bike ridership survey (nhbh-yj57) asked riders why they ride (multi-select): 87.3% cited recreation/leisure, 47.5% transportation trips, and 42.1% commuting to work/school, showing recreational enjoyment is the most widespread motivation among riders.
supporting_evidence.source_title: Bike Ridership - Edmonton Insight Community, dataset nhbh-yj57
supporting_evidence.establishes: Establishes rider motivations in an opt-in panel, though reasons per person do not measure trip purpose counts.

supporting_evidence.finding: Automated counters on river valley and shared-use paths carry roughly half of all recorded bicycle counts in Edmonton (49.96% across 28 counters in Jan-Jul 2026), demonstrating heavy recreational corridor usage.
supporting_evidence.establishes: Establishes path traffic volumes, though physical location does not establish trip purpose.

supporting_evidence.finding: The 2015 Household Travel Survey reports an average City bicycle trip length of 4.1 km (compared to 9.4 km for drivers and 9.2 km for transit), matching the 'usually within a short distance' observation.

challenging_evidence.finding: Reviewer derivation from Table 3-10 of the 2015 HTS Summary Report indicates work trips (~21,379, 37.8%-39.0% of bicycle trips) exceed home-based social/recreational trips (~11,994, 21.2%-21.9%), challenging the recreational majority claim.
challenging_evidence.source_title: 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey Summary Report, Table 3-10
challenging_evidence.establishes: Derived estimates indicate commuting trips outnumber recreational trips, refuting a recreational majority.

challenging_evidence.finding: Automated counters on protected on-street bike lanes exhibit pronounced weekday morning (08:00) and afternoon (16:00-17:00) commute peaks, with weekday traffic exceeding weekend traffic by 40% to 87% (e.g. 102 Ave E of 121 St averaged 1,040 weekday vs 557.5 weekend bikes/day in July 2025).
challenging_evidence.establishes: Demonstrates strong utilitarian commuting patterns on protected on-street bike lanes.

HTS purpose categories include School, Post-Secondary Education, Shopping, and Personal Business, which cannot be mapped cleanly onto recreation or commuting.
Counter temporal distributions (rush hour peaks) indicate utility commuting behaviour but cannot measure individual trip purpose.

The proportion of river-valley trail trips that serve utilitarian commuting.
